22:                                            Abstract
23:                                                Many conjectures and open problems in graph theory can either be reduced to cubic
24:                                            graphs or are directly stated for cubic graphs. Furthermore, it is known that for a lot of
25:                                            problems, a counterexample must be a snark, i.e. a bridgeless cubic graph which is not
26:                                            3–edge-colourable. In this paper we deal with the fact that the family of potential coun-
27:                                            terexamples to many interesting conjectures can be narrowed even further to the family
28:                                            S≥5 of bridgeless cubic graphs whose edge set cannot be covered with four perfect match-
29:                                            ings. The Cycle Double Cover Conjecture, the Shortest Cycle Cover Conjecture and the
30:                                            Fan-Raspaud Conjecture are examples of statements for which S≥5 is crucial.
31:                                                In this paper, we study parameters which have the potential to further refine S≥5 and
32:                                            thus enlarge the set of cubic graphs for which the mentioned conjectures can be verified.
33:                                            We show that S≥5 can be naturally decomposed into subsets with increasing complexity,
34:                                            thereby producing a natural scale for proving these conjectures. More precisely, we con-
35:                                            sider the following parameters and questions: given a bridgeless cubic graph, (i) how many
36:                                            perfect matchings need to be added, (ii) how many copies of the same perfect matching
37:                                            need to be added, and (iii) how many 2–factors need to be added so that the resulting reg-
38:                                            ular graph is Class I? We present new results for these parameters and we also establish
39:                                            some strong relations between these problems and some long-standing conjectures.
40:                                            Keywords: Cubic graph, edge-colouring, perfect matching index, shortest cycle cover, snark.

53: 1   Motivation
54: It is well-known that many long standing conjectures in graph theory can be reduced to
55: the class of cubic graphs. That is, if one can prove such a conjecture for all cubic graphs
56: then the general statement for arbitrary graphs will immediately follow. The Cycle Dou-
57: ble Cover Conjecture [32] and the 5–Flow Conjecture [29] fall into this category. Some
58: other well-known conjectures are formulated directly for cubic graphs such as the Petersen
59: Colouring Conjecture [18] and the Berge-Fulkerson Conjecture [10].
60:      In all mentioned conjectures, only a very small subset of all cubic graphs is critical
61: for proving them. A classical result by Vizing [31] naturally divides cubic graphs in two
62: classes. More precisely, Vizing’s Theorem divides simple graphs in two classes according
63: to the value of the chromatic index χ0 with respect to the maximum degree ∆. A simple
64: graph G has χ0 (G) either equal to ∆(G) or to ∆(G) + 1, and is said to be a Class I or Class
65: II graph, respectively. In case of multigraphs G, we say that G is Class I if χ0 (G) = ∆(G),
66: and Class II, otherwise.
67:      The bridgeless cubic graphs having chromatic index 4 will be referred to as snarks,
68: and we will denote the set of all snarks by S. It can be easily shown that the study of all
69: previously mentioned conjectures can be restricted to S, since all such conjectures are true
70: for 3–edge-colourable cubic graphs. We remark that in literature one may find a stronger
71: and more refined definition of snarks, which refers only to those graphs in S which are
72: cyclically 4–edge-connected and with girth at least 5. In this paper we shall use the broader
73: definition of snarks and shall refer to the more specifically defined snarks as non-trivial
74: snarks.
75:      In addition, the class of snarks relevant for some old and new problems can be further
76: restricted to a specific subset of S, which we shall denote by S≥5 (see definition below).
77: More precisely, S≥5 is shown to be critical for several, seemingly unrelated, problems. In

135: Conjecture, also have the largest possible circular flow number according to the 5–Flow
136: conjecture. We remark that the converse of the latter is false: there exists a large number of
137: non-trivial snarks having circular flow number 5 and perfect matching index 4 (see [13]).

91:     Secondly, the hot spots conjecture, originally formulated in the 1970s for domains,
92: roughly speaking asks for which domains (or manifolds, graphs, . . . ) the maximum
93: and minimum of the eigenfunction(s) of the first nontrivial eigenvalue of the Neu-
94: mann Laplacian are on the boundary of the domain; see, e.g., the introduction of
95: [8] for a motivation and an historical description of the problem on domains, and
96: [16] for the famous counterexample to the original conjecture. The idea behind the
97: conjecture comes from the corresponding heat equation: an expansion of solutions
98: as Fourier series in the eigenfunctions shows that the maximum and minimum of the
99: first nontrivial eigenfunctions represent the generically hottest and coldest points
100: in the domain; and as heat flow should respect the geometry of the domain, it is
101: natural to expect these points to be located far away from each in some reasonable
102: sense.
103:     The same question, or rather an adapted variant, has also been asked in the
104: case of discrete graphs: motivated in part by previous applications of the critical
105: points of the Fiedler vector(s) of a finite discrete graph to the analysis of data in
106: various contexts, in [20] the authors conjectured that its points of maximum and
107: minimum should always realise the diameter of the graph; we might call this a
108: version of the hot spots conjecture for discrete graphs. As it turns out, there are
109: fairly simple counterexamples, even among tree graphs, as first exhibited in [22].
110: But the principle that the graph hot spots should represent an analytic, weighted

115: version of the diameter is intuitively reasonable, and finding classes of graphs for
116: which the graph version of the hot spots conjecture holds (and understanding better
117: the extent to which it fails) is a topic of ongoing research; we refer to [24, 39] and
118: in particular [37].
119:     These same motivations remain valid in the case of quantum graphs, where, as
120: mentioned, very little is known. Our principal goal here is thus to understand
121: better how the “hot and cold spots” of a quantum graph, more precisely the global,
122: and also local, maxima and minima of the first nontrivial eigenfunction(s) of the
123: standard Laplacian, the natural quantum graph analogue of both the Neumann and

101:    Secondly, the hot spots conjecture, originally formulated in the 1970s for domains,
102: roughly speaking asks for which domains (or manifolds, graphs, . . . ) the maximum
103: and minimum of the eigenfunction(s) of the first nontrivial eigenvalue of the Neu-
104: mann Laplacian are on the boundary of the domain; see, e.g., the introduction
105: of [15] for a motivation and an historical description of the problem on domains,
106: [23] for the famous counterexample to the original conjecture, and [38, 45, 54, 55]
107: for recent advances on the problem. The idea behind the conjecture comes from
108: the corresponding heat equation: an expansion of solutions as Fourier series in the
109: eigenfunctions shows that the maximum and minimum of the first nontrivial eigen-
110: functions represent the generically hottest and coldest points in the domain; and as
111: heat flow should respect the geometry of the domain, it is natural to expect these
112: points to be located far away from each other in some reasonable sense.

22:                                            Abstract
23:                                                Many conjectures and open problems in graph theory can either be reduced to cubic
24:                                            graphs or are directly stated for cubic graphs. Furthermore, it is known that for a lot of
25:                                            problems, a counterexample must be a snark, i.e. a bridgeless cubic graph which is not
26:                                            3–edge-colourable. In this paper we deal with the fact that the family of potential coun-
27:                                            terexamples to many interesting conjectures can be narrowed even further to the family
28:                                            S≥5 of bridgeless cubic graphs whose edge set cannot be covered with four perfect match-
29:                                            ings. The Cycle Double Cover Conjecture, the Shortest Cycle Cover Conjecture and the
30:                                            Fan-Raspaud Conjecture are examples of statements for which S≥5 is crucial.
31:                                                In this paper, we study parameters which have the potential to further refine S≥5 and
32:                                            thus enlarge the set of cubic graphs for which the mentioned conjectures can be verified.
33:                                            We show that S≥5 can be naturally decomposed into subsets with increasing complexity,
34:                                            thereby producing a natural scale for proving these conjectures. More precisely, we con-
35:                                            sider the following parameters and questions: given a bridgeless cubic graph, (i) how many
36:                                            perfect matchings need to be added, (ii) how many copies of the same perfect matching
37:                                            need to be added, and (iii) how many 2–factors need to be added so that the resulting reg-
38:                                            ular graph is Class I? We present new results for these parameters and we also establish
39:                                            some strong relations between these problems and some long-standing conjectures.
40:                                            Keywords: Cubic graph, edge-colouring, perfect matching index, shortest cycle cover, snark.

53: 1   Motivation
54: It is well-known that many long standing conjectures in graph theory can be reduced to
55: the class of cubic graphs. That is, if one can prove such a conjecture for all cubic graphs
56: then the general statement for arbitrary graphs will immediately follow. The Cycle Dou-
57: ble Cover Conjecture [32] and the 5–Flow Conjecture [29] fall into this category. Some
58: other well-known conjectures are formulated directly for cubic graphs such as the Petersen
59: Colouring Conjecture [18] and the Berge-Fulkerson Conjecture [10].
60:      In all mentioned conjectures, only a very small subset of all cubic graphs is critical
61: for proving them. A classical result by Vizing [31] naturally divides cubic graphs in two
62: classes. More precisely, Vizing’s Theorem divides simple graphs in two classes according
63: to the value of the chromatic index χ0 with respect to the maximum degree ∆. A simple
64: graph G has χ0 (G) either equal to ∆(G) or to ∆(G) + 1, and is said to be a Class I or Class
65: II graph, respectively. In case of multigraphs G, we say that G is Class I if χ0 (G) = ∆(G),
66: and Class II, otherwise.
67:      The bridgeless cubic graphs having chromatic index 4 will be referred to as snarks,
68: and we will denote the set of all snarks by S. It can be easily shown that the study of all
69: previously mentioned conjectures can be restricted to S, since all such conjectures are true
70: for 3–edge-colourable cubic graphs. We remark that in literature one may find a stronger
71: and more refined definition of snarks, which refers only to those graphs in S which are
72: cyclically 4–edge-connected and with girth at least 5. In this paper we shall use the broader
73: definition of snarks and shall refer to the more specifically defined snarks as non-trivial
74: snarks.
75:      In addition, the class of snarks relevant for some old and new problems can be further
76: restricted to a specific subset of S, which we shall denote by S≥5 (see definition below).
77: More precisely, S≥5 is shown to be critical for several, seemingly unrelated, problems. In

135: Conjecture, also have the largest possible circular flow number according to the 5–Flow
136: conjecture. We remark that the converse of the latter is false: there exists a large number of
137: non-trivial snarks having circular flow number 5 and perfect matching index 4 (see [13]).

10:                                                   Abstract. The 1/3-2/3 Conjecture, originally formulated in 1968, is one of
11:                                                   the best-known open problems in the theory of posets, stating that the balance
12:                                                   constant of any non-total order is at least 1/3. By reinterpreting balance
13:                                                   constants of posets in terms of convex subsets of the symmetric group, we
14:                                                   extend the study of balance constants to convex subsets C of any Coxeter
15:                                                   group. Remarkably, we conjecture that the lower bound of 1/3 still applies in
16:                                                   any finite Weyl group, with new and interesting equality cases appearing.
17:                                                       We generalize several of the main results towards the 1/3-2/3 Conjecture to
18:                                                   this new setting: we prove our conjecture when C is a weak order interval below
19:                                                   a fully commutative element in any acyclic Coxeter group (a generalization
20:                                                   of the case of width-two posets), we give a uniform lower bound for balance
21:                                                   constants in all finite Weyl groups using a new generalization of order polytopes
22:                                                   to this context, and we introduce generalized semiorders for which we resolve
23:                                                   the conjecture.
24:                                                       We hope this new perspective may shed light on the proper level of gen-
25:                                                   erality in which to consider the 1/3-2/3 Conjecture, and therefore on which
26:                                                   methods are likely to be successful in resolving it.
